titulo: Closer or Space? The Same Evening, From Both Sides
caption: YouTube only (a medio in 16:9, no Short and no Reel). What goes out is the YouTube title and the description.
descripcion:
One evening between Ari and Cella, seen twice. First from Ari's side, wanting to be closer. Then from Cella's side, needing space. Both have a reason.

Which side was easier to understand: Ari's or Cella's?

If you searched "avoidant" or "why do I push my partner away", this is one evening of what many people describe, told from both sides. Nobody in it gets a label or a diagnosis, and it isn't advice about anyone's relationship.

The middle of the video uses one idea from research on adult attachment, the study of how adults handle closeness in relationships. Researchers describe two responses people often show when closeness feels uncertain: moving closer and checking, or making space and handling it alone. They describe both as ways of trying to feel safe, often learned in earlier relationships, with temperament playing a part too. They measure them in degrees, with questionnaires on two scales: worry about being rejected, and discomfort with closeness. This research describes patterns across many people and says little about any one person, and its account of where these responses come from has only been tested in part. What Ari and Cella do at the end is our own small idea; these studies did not test it.
Mikulincer, M., Shaver, P. R., & Pereg, D. (2003). Attachment theory and affect regulation: The dynamics, development, and cognitive consequences of attachment-related strategies. Motivation and Emotion, 27(2), 77-102. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1024515519160
The line of research on couples started with: Hazan, C., & Shaver, P. (1987). Romantic love conceptualized as an attachment process. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 52(3), 511-524.

alt: A video of about 9 minutes in 16:9 with a warm woman's voice narrating in the third person. Two small doorway-shaped figures with white eyes live together in a dark blue apartment at night: Ari, light blue, always on the left, and Cella, amber, always on the right. It opens on a hug at the front door: Ari rushes in, Cella steps back, and the screen reads Ari wanted closer. and Cella wanted space. before a split screen. Then four moments of the same evening, each shown twice, first with a band reading ARI'S SIDE and then CELLA'S SIDE, with the time in the top right: the short hug at 7:10 PM, a dinner where Ari asks Come to my sister's wedding? It's in May. and Cella says Maybe. Let's see. and reaches for her phone, a bench at 9:15 PM where Ari keeps sliding closer and texts are we ok? from across the room and gets yeah. just tired, and 10:00 PM, when Ari asks Can we talk about us?, Cella says Not tonight. and a bedroom door closes. Speech goes in bubbles; thoughts go in cards headed INSIDE ARI or INSIDE CELLA, such as Did I do something? and I need ten quiet minutes before I can be close. A split screen shows the living room and the bedroom with the same door between them. A blackboard draws the circle: Ari comes closer, Cella feels crowded, Cella steps back, Ari feels alone, with an arrow back to the top. The voice then explains a 2003 review by Mikulincer, Shaver and Pereg, with key words on screen (Closer. Space. Both: trying to feel safe. Learned earlier. Two scales. No labels here.) and what the research does not know. In the end both write on their phones: Ari, I feel far from you tonight. I'd like ten minutes with you before bed., and Cella, I need an hour alone. You did nothing wrong. I'll come out at 11 to talk. At 11 Cella comes out and sits on the bench, then moves closer herself. It ends with For the person you share evenings like this with. and Closer to yourself.
